summaries.example: Imagine seeing a red object through a strange window. The experience really is an experience of red, but you might wrongly decide that the object itself is red. Autrecourt separates what appears to us from the judgment we make about it.
summaries.summary: Nicholas of Autrecourt was a medieval philosopher whose life is known from a small number of documents. He studied and taught in places connected with Paris, later held a church position at Metz, and died in 1369. A long investigation began in 1340. He was convicted, required to reject several teachings in public, and prevented from reaching the highest teaching rank in theology. Some of his writings were burned. Autrecourt’s surviving works discuss knowledge, reality, nature, language, and ethics. He said that clear perception gives us dependable knowledge of what appears. But he denied that we can prove, just from one thing, the existence of a hidden substance or a cause behind another thing. He also proposed that nature is made of very small pieces of matter and that change happens through their movement. Scholars once labeled him a medieval skeptic, but the entry explains that this label is too simple: he defended the senses while questioning certain claims about causes and substances.
key_ideas: Nicholas of Autrecourt was a fourteenth-century thinker connected with the University of Paris.
He was put on trial and publicly rejected teachings that officials judged unacceptable.
He argued that clear sense experience can be trustworthy, but our guesses about causes and hidden substances may not be certain.
He challenged important Aristotelian ideas and defended a view in which tiny bits of matter move.
He was not simply a skeptic: he criticized ancient skeptics and defended reliable perception.
summaries.why_it_matters: Autrecourt shows that people in the Middle Ages did not all agree about Aristotle or about how knowledge works. His ideas make us ask what our senses tell us, what our reasoning can prove, and how quickly we should move from an experience to a larger claim about reality. His trial also shows that philosophical ideas could have serious consequences in a university and religious setting.

important_terms.definition: A philosopher’s study of how we know things and when our beliefs can be certain.
The rule that something cannot both be true and false in the same way at the same time.
The view that the world is made from tiny pieces of matter that move.
The idea that some things in the world are basic realities, while their changing features depend on them.

questions_to_think_about: Can seeing something clearly ever be enough for knowledge?
How can an experience be real while a judgment about the outside world is mistaken?
If two events happen one after another, does that prove that one caused the other?

summaries.example: Suppose a person observes that a struck match is followed by a flame. An Aristotelian approach might treat repeated observation as a route to knowledge of a causal relation. Autrecourt’s stricter standard asks whether the first event and the second are logically inseparable. Since one can be conceived without contradiction while denying the other, he argues that the observation does not yield certain knowledge of causality.
summaries.summary: Nicholas of Autrecourt was a fourteenth-century philosopher associated with the arts and theology faculties at Paris. Historical records indicate that he later became a canon and eventually dean at Metz, but the details of his academic status remain uncertain. Summoned to Avignon in 1340, he faced a process that ended in condemnation: a large set of propositions drawn from his writings and teaching was judged false, dangerous, erroneous, or heretical. He recanted publicly in Avignon and Paris, and his advancement to the theological magisterium was barred. His philosophical importance lies partly in his challenge to dominant Aristotelian assumptions. Autrecourt holds that evident knowledge must ultimately be grounded in the principle of non-contradiction, except for the certainty of faith. This stringent account blocks a certain inference from an effect to its cause or from perceptible accidents to an underlying substance, because distinct entities are not logically contradictory. Yet he does not doubt everything. He argues that clear sensory appearances are reliable; mistakes arise when a person forms an ontological judgment from an incomplete appearance, dream, or image. In natural philosophy he presents atomism, with indivisible parcels of matter, points, and instants, and treats motion as not a separate entity inhering in a body. His discussions also touch on the status of propositions, necessity, reference, and the complexe significabile.
key_ideas: Autrecourt’s surviving works include correspondence, the Exigit ordo, and a theological question; the Exigit is an unfinished or disordered treatise rather than a systematic commentary.
He makes the principle of non-contradiction the ultimate basis for evident knowledge, apart from the special certainty of faith.
Because distinct entities can be conceived without contradiction, he denies that knowledge of one substance or event alone proves another substance or a causal relation.
His position is not global skepticism. He treats clear sensory appearances as veridical, while locating error in judgments made from unclear appearances, dreams, or images.
In natural philosophy, he favors the greater probability of an eternal world and uses atomism to explain change, rejecting Aristotelian prime matter and substantial generation and corruption.
His condemned propositions also connect him with medieval debates about necessity, meaning, reference, and what propositions signify.
summaries.why_it_matters: Autrecourt is important because his work complicates a familiar story about medieval philosophy. He was neither a straightforward defender of Aristotelian science nor a complete skeptic. Instead, he combined confidence in clear perception with distrust of arguments that claim certainty about causality and substance. His case also illustrates how epistemology, metaphysics, natural philosophy, semantics, and institutional authority were closely connected in fourteenth-century thought. The entry cautions that later comparisons to Ockham or to modern skeptics can obscure the specific structure of Autrecourt’s own position.

important_terms.definition: The study of knowledge, including its sources, limits, and standards of certainty.
Autrecourt’s basic logical standard: a statement and its negation cannot both hold in the same respect at the same time.
The claim that some inferences are evident only when affirming the antecedent and denying the consequent would produce a contradiction.
A basic underlying reality, contrasted with its perceptible properties or accidents.
A property or feature that exists in or depends on a substance, such as a sensible quality in a body.
The view that matter consists of indivisible, extremely small parcels whose movement explains natural change.
A philosophical position claiming that knowledge or certainty is broadly unavailable; the entry says this label does not adequately describe Autrecourt.
A medieval theory about what an entire proposition signifies, distinct from the words or external things it concerns.

questions_to_think_about: Does the fact that two events are logically separable show that their causal connection cannot be known with certainty?
Is Autrecourt’s distinction between appearance and judgment a successful reply to dreams and perceptual error?
What kind of certainty, if any, can a philosophical criterion of clear perception have without a further proof?
How does atomism change the explanation of generation, corruption, motion, and the properties of bodies?
Why might a claim about the meaning of “Man is an animal” matter for theories of necessity and reference?

summaries.example: You watch a basketball bounce after hitting the floor. You are very sure that you saw the bounce. Autrecourt would ask a harder question: does seeing the first event prove with certainty that the floor caused the second? He thinks not, because the two events are different and can be thought about separately. The experience may be clear, while the claim about a hidden cause goes beyond what is immediately given.
summaries.summary: Nicholas of Autrecourt was a medieval philosopher whose career included study and teaching connected with Paris, work in theology and law, and later a church position at Metz. Our knowledge of his life comes from a small number of records, and some details about his degrees are disputed. In 1340 he was called to answer accusations before a papal court. The process ended with a condemnation. He had to reject selected teachings publicly in Avignon and Paris, and he was barred from becoming a master in theology. The entry presents Autrecourt as a thinker who questioned major parts of the Aristotelian tradition without being an all-purpose doubter. In epistemology, he treats the principle of non-contradiction as the foundation of evident knowledge, except for the special certainty of faith. Since a cause and its effect are distinct, he argues that knowledge of one does not by itself give certain knowledge of the other. The same reasoning challenges the inference from a thing’s perceptible qualities to an underlying substance. At the same time, he defends clear sensory appearances. He separates an experience from the judgment made about it: dreams and incomplete appearances can produce mistaken beliefs, but they do not show that experience itself is false. In natural philosophy, he favors an eternal universe and atomism, explaining change through moving indivisible parcels of matter. His writings also engage with debates about motion, properties, necessity, and the meaning of propositions.
key_ideas: Autrecourt wrote letters, a treatise called the Exigit ordo, and a theological question, but much of his work survives only in limited or imperfect form.
He says evident knowledge must be connected to non-contradiction, so a conclusion is certain only when denying it would conflict with what is already known.
This makes him challenge certainty about causes and substances: knowing one event or property does not automatically prove another thing behind it.
He trusts clear sense experience more than unclear appearances. A dream or misleading image can lead to a wrong judgment even though the experience itself happened.
He rejects parts of Aristotelian natural philosophy and explains change through moving atoms, while also treating space and time as made of indivisible units.
His trial and condemnation affected his career and made his ideas part of later university discussions.
summaries.why_it_matters: Autrecourt matters because he does not fit neatly into the label “medieval skeptic.” He questions whether reason can establish causal and substantial realities with certainty, yet he argues for the reliability of clear perception and attacks more radical ancient skepticism. Studying him helps readers see that medieval philosophers debated evidence, logic, perception, matter, and language in sophisticated ways. His condemnation also provides historical context for how philosophical disagreements could be examined and punished by academic and religious authorities.

important_terms.definition: The study of knowledge and how people can tell when a belief is certain or well supported.
The logical idea that the same thing cannot both be true and false in the same respect at the same time.
A basic thing or reality that has properties, such as a body that has color or warmth.
A changeable property of a thing, such as color, heat, or coldness, in the traditional medieval framework.
The theory that matter is made of very tiny indivisible pieces that move.
Doubt about whether knowledge or certainty is possible. The entry says Autrecourt’s doubt was limited, not universal.
A medieval discussion of what a whole sentence means, beyond the meanings of its individual words.

questions_to_think_about: Is observing a regular pattern enough to prove a cause?
Why might Autrecourt trust a clear appearance but not every conclusion drawn from it?
Could someone reject certain knowledge of causality without doubting ordinary experiences?
What advantages and problems might come with explaining change using atoms?
Why would philosophers care whether a sentence can be true when no objects of its kind exist?
